notes: Deep taproot: plant small and never move it. Emerges late, so mark the spot.
Tolerates ordinary garden soil despite the name. Best milkweed for a tidy bed.
Fine needle foliage, spreads by rhizome: a useful late-season monarch host.
Highly rhizomatous. Use only in large informal beds or a dedicated waystation.
Shrub-like mound holds form all season. Black seedpods rattle in winter. Very long lived.
Charcoal stems and white spires: the strongest vertical accent in a prairie planting.
Leave seedheads for goldfinches. Use the straight species, not double-flowered cultivars.
Drooping narrow rays, earlier than E. purpurea. Superb in lean soil.
Long bloom and a clean basal rosette. The cultivar Goldsturm is this species.
Biennial or short-lived: treat it as a self-sowing filler that knits a young bed together.
Huge blue-grey paddle leaves plus 7-foot flower stems. A signature botanical-garden plant.
Late, airy and fragrant. The cultivar Henry Eilers has distinctive quilled rays.
Very long bloom and tolerates clay. Cut back by half in June to limit height.
Velvety grey leaves. Rhizomatous: give it room or edge it with a mown strip.
The latest sunflower: a wall of gold in October. Pinch in early summer for sturdier stems.
One of very few sunflowers for dry part shade: excellent at a woodland edge.
Enormous basal leaves like elephant ears, with flowers on nearly leafless 8-foot stalks.
Deeply cut leaves orient north-south. A taproot to 14 feet deep makes it extremely drought proof.
Fused leaves hold rainwater that birds drink. Self-sows freely: deadhead in small beds.
Anise-scented seedheads. Airy enough to weave between stiffer plants.
Short lived but reseeds. Reads as a cloud of tiny sombreros in dry beds.
Plant in drifts of seven or more: single corms read as stray bottle brushes.
Button-like heads spaced along the stem. The best liatris for sand and gravel.
Shortgrass-prairie species with a 15-foot taproot. Ideal for hot dry hellstrips.
Threadlike foliage forms a neat tuft: a refined front-of-bed liatris.
A magnet for bumblebees and hummingbird clearwing moths. Give it airflow to limit mildew.
The best red for hummingbirds in moist part shade. Spreads by stolons.
Earliest, shortest and tidiest beebalm, with good mildew resistance and red fall colour.
Tiered pagoda bracts. A top plant for solitary wasps and specialist bees in sand.
Silvery bracts and the heaviest insect traffic of any eastern perennial. Rhizomatous.
A cloud of fine texture, better behaved than P. muticum in small beds.
Near-evergreen rosette, red-tinted in Husker Red. Mahogany seed spikes persist into winter.
Compact and drought tough: good on rock ledges and in gravel gardens.
Candelabra spires with whorled leaves: the classic vertical for a naturalistic border.
Tolerates drier shade than the other Joe Pyes. Domed heads swarm with butterflies.
For rain gardens and pond edges. The cultivar Gateway is a sturdier 5-foot form.
Intense violet in late summer, superb against yellow Helianthus and Solidago.
Willowy needle foliage all season. Iron Butterfly is the common selection.
Clump forming, not running: the goldenrod for a designed bed. A keystone genus.
The cultivar Fireworks sprays horizontally. A keystone genus for Lepidoptera.
Tiny, grey and tough. Thrives where nothing else will, including pure sand.
Arching blue-purple stems with flowers in the leaf axils. A true shade goldenrod.
Spreads gently into a groundcover in dry woodland shade. Broad toothed leaves.
Flat-topped heads and paddle leaves. Reliably upright, superb seed for juncos.
Cut back by half in June for a self-supporting dome. A keystone genus.
The latest and most drought tolerant aster: a neat blue cushion in October.
Smooth blue-green foliage resists mildew. Bluebird is a strong selection.
A haze of pale blue in woodland shade when almost nothing else is flowering.
Fine heather-like texture smothered in tiny white daisies. Snow Flurry is a mat form.
Dark foliage in Lady in Black. Horizontal branching fills gaps at woodland edges.
The best flowering groundcover for dry shade under trees. Spreads politely.
A fine-textured mat, extremely long blooming. Shear lightly after the first flush.
Early, cheerful and short lived. Lets you fill a new bed cheaply from seed.
Eight feet of bamboo-like stem topped with small daisies: see-through height at the back.
Stiff three-lobed leaves make a tidy rhizomatous colony. Very drought proof.
A nitrogen fixer with fine ferny leaves and glowing magenta thimbles. Bee gold.
The cool white counterpart to D. purpurea. Both excel in lean gravelly soil.
A subshrub with silver-grey ferny foliage and violet spikes with orange anthers.
A robust legume for restoration-style plantings. Spreads by rhizome in good soil.
Silvery buttons turn rich brown and hold all winter. Quail and sparrow seed.
Low arching sprays of cream flowers in mid-spring, long before other prairie plants.
A yucca-like blue-green rosette with golf-ball flower heads. Unmatched winter silhouette.
Flat white heads like a native yarrow, blooming for months. Very sturdy.
Nodding pink umbels above grassy tufts. Deer and rabbit proof, excellent in gravel.
Upright starry umbels later than A. cernuum. Seedheads dry to parchment tan.
The earliest yellow in a native border and a key nectar source for small spring bees.
Choose mildew-resistant selections such as Jeana, which also draws the most butterflies.
A fragrant spring pink that weaves through short grasses. Underused and tough.
Evergreen needle mat for edges and walls. Needs sharp drainage and no mulch.
Aggressively rhizomatous in rich moist soil. Use in rain gardens or choose Miss Manners.
The purest sky blue of autumn. Pinch it twice before July or it will lean.
Each flower lasts a morning but bloom continues for weeks. Cut back after flowering.
An iris relative that looks like a grass tuft with tiny blue stars. A front-of-bed staple.
Trailing stems with electric magenta cups. A big taproot: place it once, permanently.
Huge lemon cups on a low sprawl. Requires lean, very well drained soil.
A waxy blue-grey rosette and big tubular bells. Needs sand or gravel to persist.
The sole host of the Baltimore Checkerspot. Wants consistently moist soil in part shade.
Glossy dark leaves and hooded pink flowers. Hot Lips is a reliable selection.
The single best hummingbird plant in eastern North America. Keep it moist; it reseeds.
A bumblebee favourite for rain gardens. Short lived but self-sows into gaps.
Strong vertical blades for pond edges and rain garden bottoms. Rhizomatous.
Architectural 5-foot white bottlebrushes lighting up deep shade. Slow but permanent.
Arrives exactly with the ruby-throated hummingbird migration. Self-sows charmingly.
A reliable spring groundcover for dressed woodland shade, with good red fall colour.
Fragrant sheets of pale blue with the spring ephemerals. Blue Moon is superb.
A true stoloniferous mat for shade: better groundcover than P. divaricata, less bloom.
Semi-evergreen mottled leaves with foamy white spires. Runs gently by stolon.
The heat- and humidity-proof heuchera, with large maple-shaped semi-evergreen leaves.
Marbled evergreen rosettes, excellent for dry shade edging and containers.
Ladder-like foliage and nodding blue bells. Goes semi-dormant in late summer drought.
Evergreen rosettes spread into a weed-suppressing carpet, then throw up yellow domes.
Big heart-shaped leaves form a lush deciduous carpet. Flowers hide at ground level.
A miniature iris that creeps over the soil surface. Plant rhizomes barely covered.
Scarlet tubes flaring to yellow stars: a hummingbird plant that thrives in shade.
A spring ephemeral: fully dormant by July, so pair it with ferns that fill the gap.
Umbrella colonies of tropical-looking leaves. Dormant by late summer in dry shade.
Twisted yellow bells dangle from arching perfoliate stems. Elegant and slow.
Plumes of white become ruby berries. A strong arching form for the shade middle ground.
Large basal leaves carpet dry shade, with lavender daisies on tall stems in late summer.
Evergreen, deer proof and tolerant of dry shade and slopes. The workhorse eastern fern.
A blue-green evergreen vase, excellent in rocky dry shade. Very long lived.
Lacy, fast to fill and forgiving. Cut spent fronds in late summer if they brown.
Wiry black stems and fan-shaped fronds. Wants humus and reliable moisture.
Big architectural vases for wet shade: the structural fern of a rain garden.
Spreads fast in wet soil. Use it to colonise difficult wet shade, not small beds.
The defining evergreen fern of the coastal Northwest. Drought tolerant in deep shade.
A two-tone fern with a sterile rosette and upright fertile fronds. Needs moisture and shade.
Fast, lush and heat proof: the best deciduous fern for the Gulf South and Florida.
Glossy bronze new growth, spreading by rhizome in moist acid shade.
A genuinely drought-proof evergreen fern for rocky shade in the desert Southwest.
A silvery-woolly lip fern that curls in drought and revives with rain. For dry shaded rock.
A leathery evergreen fern spreading by rhizome in moist Florida shade. Bronze new growth.
Blue-green in summer, copper-orange in winter with silver seed. The best matrix grass.
An emerald fountain with coriander-scented flowers, turning apricot. Elegant, long lived.
Oat-like seeds hang along one side of the stem. Fast, tough and fine textured.
Eyebrow-shaped seedheads on a low turf-like tuft. The shortgrass prairie matrix.
Turkey-foot seedheads at 6 feet tall with wine-red autumn colour. Use compact selections in beds.
Bronze-gold plumes catch low autumn light. More strictly upright than big bluestem.
Airy pink flower clouds and stiff winter stems. Northwind is the best upright form.
A rose-pink smoke cloud in October. Needs sharp drainage and full sun to flower well.
Undaunted is a compact, extremely drought tolerant pink-flowering muhly for hot beds.
A big sculptural fountain with spike-like flower stems. The backbone grass of the Southwest.
A big glossy fountain with rose-purple plumes: rare among grasses for desert part shade.
A fine upright fountain that holds its shape all winter. Excellent in dry filtered shade.
Flat dangling oat spikelets, one of very few showy shade grasses. Reseeds vigorously.
A low purple-pink fog in late summer. Short lived; let it move around the bed.
The premier dry-shade green mulch: a soft lawn-like carpet under oaks. Rhizomatous.
A hair-fine clumping sedge for dry shade, reading as a soft green mist. No mowing.
Wide, ribbed, puckered evergreen leaves: a bold-textured groundcover for rich shade.
Ultra-fine bright green cushions, happy on limestone and in dry rooty shade.
Broad glaucous blue leaves for moist Southeastern shade. Evergreen in mild winters.
Forms raised tussocks in standing water. The structural sedge for rain garden bottoms.
A very drought tolerant clumping woodland sedge, good in root-filled dry shade.
A rhizomatous sedge used as a low-water lawn alternative on the West Coast.
A tough evergreen wetland sedge for Northwest rain gardens and swales.
A graceful arching sedge with dangling beaked seed. An excellent tall matrix for shade.
A tough clumping sedge for the cool-season matrix of a plains planting. Star-shaped seed.
The groundcover answer for dry shade under live oak and juniper in Texas. Needs no water.
A fine blue-grey bunchgrass, the matrix of Northwest and Rocky Mountain dry meadows.
A big blue-grey fountain that tolerates dry shade under oaks. A superb matrix grass.
The California state grass. Deep rooted, summer dormant, with awns that catch light.
Shimmering airy flower clouds. One of the best grasses for part shade and moist soil.
Long twisting awns glow silver. The signature grass of the northern shortgrass plains.
A reddish-purple seed haze on a small tuft. Blooms twice with summer rain in the desert.
A blue-grey dune grass that laughs at salt spray and shifting sand. Dewey Blue is the garden form.
Silvery-white flower clouds on a tidy blue-green fountain. Very salt tolerant.
A lush evergreen mound of arching blades. The best structural native grass for South Florida.
Bracts form crisp white stars for months. Reads as a flower but behaves as a wetland sedge.
Fragrant white tassels then brilliant scarlet fall colour held into December. Suckers gently.
Use lacecap forms such as Haas Halo: the mophead Annabelle offers pollinators nothing.
Bold oak-shaped leaves, burgundy fall colour, exfoliating bark. A four-season anchor.
Powerfully fragrant midsummer spikes in shade. One of the best shrubs for wet soil.
Honey-scented spring bottlebrushes and blazing orange-red fall colour on a neat mound.
A nitrogen-fixing dwarf shrub for dry lean soil, with huge insect visitation for its size.
Gro-Low is a 2 feet tall by 8 feet wide bank cover with scarlet fall colour and fruit for birds.
A keystone genus. Needs acid soil. Edible fruit and a crimson autumn carpet.
Glossy leaves, black fruit for winter birds, wine-red fall colour. Very adaptable.
Exfoliating bark and clusters of white flowers. Choose green forms over dark cultivars.
A suckering low shrub that thrives in dry shade where little else will grow.
Host of the spicebush swallowtail. Chartreuse early flowers, clear yellow fall colour.
Startling magenta fruit clusters in autumn, heavily used by mockingbirds and thrashers.
The native evergreen alternative to boxwood. Shamrock and Gem Box are compact selections.
A tiny leadplant for the coldest, driest gravel beds, with fine silver-green foliage.
Coral-pink fruit clings all winter. Thrives in dry shade; suckers into thickets.
White berries persist into winter. Among the most shade- and drought-tolerant native shrubs.
Aromatic semi-evergreen that fixes nitrogen; the waxy fruit is key winter food for warblers.
Scarlet winter stems, white fruit for birds. A keystone genus; coppice a third of the stems yearly.
A hardy evergreen fan palm giving subtropical botanical-garden structure in deep shade.
Silver-blue evergreen fans give year-round structure. The fruit is critical wildlife food.
The sole host of the atala butterfly. A glossy evergreen cycad rosette for sun or shade.
Orange tubes almost year-round for hummingbirds and zebra longwings. Use the native species.
A glossy evergreen hedge shrub with edible fruit. Salt and wind tolerant.
Glossy corrugated evergreen leaves and red fruit. The definitive shrub for South Florida shade.
The most reliable blue penstemon for cold dry gardens, with a semi-evergreen rosette.
Needle foliage and scarlet tubes for months. Superb in gravel with Zauschneria.
The earliest hummingbird plant on the Colorado Plateau. Needs lean soil.
The only fragrant penstemon: 5-foot spires of pink snapdragons over blue-grey leaves.
Months of bloom in hot dry sites. Short lived but reseeds; deadhead for more flowers.
Root-beer scented grey foliage and salmon tubes. Hummingbirds defend it fiercely.
Anise-scented, blooms for three months and hums with bees. Self-sows moderately.
Lavender-blue daisies with yellow eyes in early summer. Easy and long lived.
Buckwheats host an enormous range of butterflies. Flowers age from sulphur to rust.
Fresh blue saucers every morning on wiry stems. Reseeds to drift through gravel.
A silvery mound covered in small gold daisies through the worst heat and drought.
Deeply cut leaves with fine red fall colour. A meadow staple of the northern Rockies.
A mound of gold in autumn when the desert has little else. Silver-grey stems in winter.
White roses followed by pink feathery seed plumes that glow backlit for months.
A keystone genus. Early white flowers, edible fruit, orange fall colour. Multi-stemmed.
A low evergreen holly-like carpet for dry shade in the interior West. Blue fruit.
The Colorado state flower. Needs afternoon shade and even moisture at low elevation.
Clove-scented yellow flowers, edible fruit, scarlet fall colour. Very drought tolerant.
Columbine-like blue-green foliage and airy flowers for Rocky Mountain shade gardens.
Silver-grey felted leaves and apricot cups nearly year-round with occasional water.
Blooms almost continuously on woolly white foliage. Short lived but reseeds readily.
A silver-white dome that erupts in gold daisies each spring. Emblem of the Sonoran Desert.
Evergreen, resinous, essentially immortal, and host to many specialist desert bees.
A silver-grey trailing mat: the best low-water groundcover for hot Southwestern beds.
An airy ferny shrub that turns purple in autumn and swarms with bees. Very drought proof.
A neat white-daisy cushion blooming most of the year. Demands perfect drainage.
A rhizomatous six-inch mat solid with papery gold flowers. Thrives on pure neglect.
A silver mound with a haze of tiny flowers aging to rust. A key desert butterfly host.
An aromatic evergreen needle mound topped with gold daisies. Excellent in limestone gravel.
An evergreen strappy fountain with 5-foot coral spikes. A hummingbird magnet all summer.
A perfect blue-grey artichoke rosette: the strongest single focal form in a desert bed.
A silver-blue sphere of fine leaves atop a trunk. Cold hardy and strongly architectural.
An evergreen grass-like fountain that reads as a grass but never needs cutting back.
The key monarch host across the arid Southwest. Sprawling clumps with chartreuse umbels.
Smells distinctly of cocoa each morning. Green-backed maroon discs after the petals drop.
A nearly everblooming lavender mat in the desert Southwest. Shear to refresh it.
Blooms spring to frost. The essential hummingbird subshrub of Texas and the Southwest.
Violet spikes over grey-green leaves for most of the year. Tough and self-sowing.
Butterfly-like flowers dance on wiry stems for months. Use as an airy veil, not a mass.
An evergreen grassy tuft with gold daisies on bare stems nearly all year. Tiny and tough.
Glossy leathery leaves and rose-red tubes on limestone. Blooms through summer heat.
Blooms in the worst heat of a Texas summer, with fine twiggy winter structure.
Scarlet trumpets from summer to frost in filtered shade. A top Southwestern hummingbird shrub.
Blue-grey evergreen holly-like foliage, fragrant early flowers, red fruit. Deer proof.
Blooms from spring to frost with no irrigation. Tough enough for part shade under mesquite.
Blooms and fruits at once for months in dry shade. Translucent red berries feed birds.
Furled scarlet turbans all summer in deep shade. The premier hummingbird plant for Southern shade.
Scarlet whorls over scalloped leaves in dry limestone shade. Reseeds gently into colonies.
Tiny fiery red peppers that mockingbirds strip. A rare fruiting shrub for dry shade.
Long-spurred gold flowers for shaded canyon-style beds. Surprisingly long blooming.
A true Arizona and New Mexico native: coral bells over evergreen rosettes in mountain shade.
A reseeding annual that fills a young bed with orange silk. Never fertilise or water it.
The fragrance carries thirty feet on a warm evening. Whorled flower stalks dry to rattles.
One of very few plants that spreads by rhizome in dry California shade. Fruity scent.
Luminous white evergreen foliage makes a strong pale accent. Absolutely no summer water.
Erupts scarlet exactly when hummingbirds need fuel in late summer. Rhizomatous.
A keystone of California scrub, supporting an extraordinary range of bees and butterflies.
Grey-green rosettes with rose pompoms. The perfect small-scale buckwheat for a front edge.
Apricot trumpets over glossy resinous leaves. Blooms with essentially no summer water.
An evergreen blue-flowered bank cover. Yankee Point is the standard selection.
A keystone genus. Glossy evergreen carpet with mahogany stems and urn-shaped flowers.
Evergreen with heavy red winter fruit for robins and waxwings. Screens beautifully.
Evergreen fans spread into colonies in coastal part shade. Many named hybrids exist.
Large evergreen rosettes for dry California shade, with long-blooming pink sprays.
The go-to evergreen groundcover for dry shade under California oaks.
The first nectar for returning rufous hummingbirds. Pendant pink tassels in late winter.
A powerfully minty grey mound with lavender pincushions. Extremely popular with bees.
Thick evergreen paddles and lavender daisies. Thrives in wind, salt and poor soil.
Late violet daisies, rhizomatous, tolerant of clay and coastal exposure.
The primary monarch host for western California. Rhizomatous; dies back hard in autumn.
Big velvety grey leaves and dramatic pink stars. A key western monarch host. Spreads.
Silver palmate leaves and violet spires. Short lived, spectacular, and fixes nitrogen.
A ferny mat with flat landing-pad flowers for tiny wasps and beneficial insects. Use local genotypes.
Blue stars over grassy fans in late winter and spring, then summer dormant.
Pigeon Point is a tough evergreen bank cover. Late bloom feeds an extraordinary range of insects.
The western counterpart to cardinal flower: scarlet tubes for seeps, swales and shaded pond edges.
The Oregon state flower: holly-like evergreen, yellow flowers, blue fruit, bronze winter tint.
A low evergreen carpet for dry conifer shade where almost nothing grows. Very slow.
A keystone genus: leathery evergreen understory shrub with edible blue-black fruit.
Bronze new growth on glossy evergreen tiers. A keystone genus with excellent fruit.
Foaming cream plumes age to tan and persist all winter. Very drought tolerant.
Rose-pink spires for wet ground. Suckers freely: ideal for swales and pond edges.
Nodding red-and-yellow lanterns in dappled shade. A key western hummingbird plant.
A blue-green ferny carpet with pink lockets. Spreads by rhizome, dormant in summer drought.
Scalloped semi-evergreen leaves and tall fringed bells. Reliable in Northwest shade.
A lush clover-like carpet for deep moist shade under conifers. Folds its leaves in bright sun.
A glossy evergreen heart-shaped carpet with curious long-tailed flowers at ground level.
Delicate duck-foot leaves on wiry stems, spreading into a fine mat in dry shade.
A bulb for soil that is wet in spring and dry in summer. Naturalises into blue rivers.
A woolly silver mound topped with gold daisies. Needs lean soil and no summer irrigation.
Pink mallow cups on a low spreading plant. A host for painted lady relatives.
The easiest penstemon west of the Cascades: tolerates real garden moisture and clay.
A glossy evergreen strawberry runner: a tough walkable groundcover for sun or part shade.
Evergreen grassy cushions with pink drumsticks. Genuinely thrives in wind and salt spray.
A powder-blue autumn haze swarming with small butterflies. Rhizomatous: give it room.
Blooms virtually year-round in Florida. Reseeds into gaps; the top hummingbird annual.
The Florida state wildflower. Nearly everblooming; self-sows to drift through a bed.
Silvery silky grass-like tufts all year, then gold daisies in autumn. Superb edging.
A salt- and sand-proof reseeding annual for coastal and Gulf beds. Continuous bloom.
A monarch host for wet shade, evergreen in the Deep South, blooming for months.
A low lavender-flowered mat, host for the common buckeye. A true Florida groundcover.
Do not confuse with invasive Mexican petunia. This native host blooms for months.
Large lavender-blue fringed daisies over evergreen rosettes. An excellent Southeastern edger.
Slender wands of purple in sandhill gardens in autumn. Excellent in pure sand.
A sprawling everblooming sunflower for hot sand and salt: effectively a flowering groundcover.
A salt-proof succulent-leaved goldenrod. Critical autumn fuel for monarchs on the coastal flyway.
The prairie alumroot: takes full prairie sun as well as part shade. Very cold hardy.
Arching stems with dangling bells, then blue-black berries. Clear yellow fall colour in shade.
The best blue aster for limestone part shade, arching gracefully out of a woodland edge.
A vigorously rhizomatous white-flowered carpet. Use it to hold difficult moist ground.
Nodding pink bells become feathery smoke-pink seedheads over a semi-evergreen rosette.
A keystone host genus for fritillary butterflies. It will colonise: use it as lawn and bed groundcover.
A fast-running edible groundcover and high-value host genus. Excellent green mulch in sun.
A flat silver evergreen mat for poor dry soil and paths. Host to the American lady butterfly.
The only eastern sedum for shade: a succulent evergreen carpet over rock, logs and dry slopes.
A tiny evergreen vine forming flat mats in acid shade, with paired fragrant flowers and red fruit.
Fine needle texture all summer, then pure gold in autumn. Perennial Plant of the Year 2011.
A shrub-like blue-green mound with steel-blue spring flowers and gold fall colour.
Dinner-plate flowers in wet soil, and the sole host of the specialist rose-mallow bee.
For standing water to 12 inches deep. Host of specialist Melissodes bees; glossy arrow-shaped leaves.
A candelabra of violet spikes for wet sun. Specialist bee host; goldfinches strip the seed.
Towering but graceful, and one of the best tall perennials for moist part shade.
